summary: A small light on St. Peters Island in Hillsborough Bay, off Charlottetown: its first lit tower dates from 1881; the lighthouse is federally owned and best seen from the water.

structures.type: square tapered wooden tower with lantern and gallery
structures.note: Lighthouse Friends says this tower is active again; the Society says the tower now in use replaced the 1964 cylinder
tower in use, per the Society's technical data; the Society's history says it was built in the 1980s

access.note: Owned by the Canadian Coast Guard or the Government of Canada (sources differ). Lighthouse Friends lists the grounds open and the tower closed. Not visible from land; best seen by boat or from the air (Society).

events.note: £32 paid for erecting a light on the island; oil also paid for that year; the type of light is not known (Journal of the House of Assembly of PEI for 1866, as cited by Lighthouse Friends)
Work begun by Joseph Egan under a contract for $500; total spent $765.87
Fixed white light, put into operation at the opening of navigation in 1881
Fixed white changed to fixed red, to avoid confusion with Blockhouse Point and Point Prim lights
Moved about a mile south-east to the south side of the island, winter 1883-84 (Directory gives 1884)
8-inch pressed glass lens and Hincks duplex burner lamp
Fixed red changed to occulting white, showing six seconds in thirty
Keeper James J. Taylor fell at the lighthouse on 9 November; a substitute was in charge from 13 November while he was treated for an infected ankle
Made an unwatched electric light on 3 October 1947
Light moved to a metal cylinder resembling a culvert pipe
Replacement tower similar to the original; the Society's history says the 1980s, its data gives 1990

corrections.why: Lighthouse Friends says the 1881 tower is active again, and the Society's technical data says Status: Active. Rowlett's current page is mixed: its heading says 'Inactive but listed', while its text says the light has been returned to the original tower. The status is disputed; the proposed value follows the two most specific descriptions.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Rowlett's directory dates the station's establishment to 1866. Lighthouse Friends shows the 1866 money was for a light of unknown type, and the lit tower dates from the opening of navigation in 1881. The record's 1866 is the station's establishment, not a known lighting.
The 1881 date is the lit tower built under Joseph Egan's 1880 contract (Lighthouse Friends). The 1866 date reflects the first money spent on a light. Both are supported.

notes_for_editor: Thin-to-moderate evidence: no storms or wrecks were found for this station in the corpus or on the web. Disagreements: (1) which tower stands now: Lighthouse Friends says the 1881 tower is active again; Rowlett's text says the light has been returned to the original tower, under a heading that says inactive; the Society says the tower in use dates from the 1980s and its data gives 1990. The record's 11.5 m height matches neither exactly (Lighthouse Friends gives 11.6 m for the 1881 tower, the Society 9.1 m for the current tower). (2) Range: the Society gives 10 nautical miles; the record gives 8. Focal height: the record gives 21.0 m, the Society 20.6 m, Rowlett 21 m. The record's 8 nm and 21 m figures come from Wikidata and the French Wikipedia; not verified here. (3) Lighthouse Friends' keepers text reads 'James W. Taylor was keeper from 1787 to 1912', an evident typo for 1897. (4) The Marine keeper table for fiscal 1909-10 (scan p.255, printed p.253) was read on the page image: 'St. Peters Island | James W. Taylor | May 1, 1897 | 400.00'. The OCR had garbled the first name; the image confirms it. (5) The Marine keeper table for fiscal 1913-14 (scan p.69, printed p.62) was read on the page image: 'St. Peters island | J. J. Taylor | June 15, 1912' and 'St. Peters range | J. McGrath' are separate rows. (6) The Society's list of James MacGrath (1913) and William Geldert (1939) is not confirmed by Lighthouse Friends or the Marine tables; the 1913-14 J. McGrath is at St. Peters range, a different station, and is not linked to this one. (7) The Island Register page (a private Taylor family genealogy, islandregister.com/taylor4.html) was read; it names private family members, including someone described as a lighthouse keeper, but nothing links them to this station's keepers. It is not used. (8) French Wikipedia (leads only, not cited) gives a 1984 relocation and a 5-second period; it conflicts with Lighthouse Friends' 1883-84 and the Society's 4-second flash. (9) The 1945 substitute's start date comes from Lighthouse Friends; its end date is missing in the source. (10) Canadian newspapers are not in the search tools here; a PEI newspaper search could add storms or the 1945 incident. (11) The Parks Canada heritage register was not checked; the community petition is from the Society only. (12) Name clash: St. Peters Harbour Light (Kings County, on St. Peter's Bay, a different station) appears in the same Marine keeper tables and in search results; none of its entries is used here, and the 'St. Peters range' and 'St. Peters Harbour' rows in the 1910 and 1914 tables are not this station. (13) 1866: the sources give money for erecting a light and station establishment in 1866, but no source says the light was lit that year; the story reports the money without calling it the first lighting.
